rv.q: This is Oklahoma! for an era in which longstanding American legacies are being examined with newly skeptical eyes.
Oklahoma! has us all at the barn dance.
This Oklahoma! is no stuffy academic revisionist exercise — it’s a theatrical blow-out.
This Oklahoma! is a thrilling reinvention that makes Rodgers and Hammerstein's 1943 musical feel urgent and contemporary while honoring its enduring emotional truths.
The wonder of this production is that so much of the joy and optimism of the original work still shines bright through the darkness.
This is a production that takes the familiar and makes it feel dangerous again
This Oklahoma! is not your grandmother's Oklahoma! – and that's exactly the point of Daniel Fish's stark, brilliant reimagining of the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic.
What’s best in this “Oklahoma!” is the morally ambiguous cue Fish develops so smartly from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s own narrative impulses.

Where intentional or not, Fish and his unforgiving team of designers have forged an "Oklahoma" for a digital America where everyone has their confirmatory feeds and dealing with another human can mean starring down the barrel of a gun.
Too often I found myself weighing the moments of inspiration against the moments of bewildering distraction.
Everything you cherish about this classic has been taken out behind the barn and shot, replaced by an auteur’s bag of tricks and a thesis on gun control and westward expansion.

That darkness is not just confined to one scene but is spiritually draped over Daniel Fish’s daring, brilliant, utterly absorbing re-interpretation of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s 1943 musical play; a first in itself.
On Broadway, Daniel Fish’s Oklahoma! has reached its full potential.

"A crazily experimental theatrical experience...But this revival of ‘Oklahoma!’ happens to be terrific fun, too...The ensemble’s interactions are casual, loose, wiry, and scrappy, with an energetic sense of anticipation, and their singing, while full-throated, can also be raw...
This Oklahoma! is unquestionably a triumph, one that honors Rodgers and Hammerstein's original while making it feel urgent and necessary for today.
This makes it the most engrossing musical currently on Broadway and a must-see.
And the local production was a theatrical treat for audiences who were able to take advantage of the unusual opportunity.
This is not only a fascinating deconstruction of the original musical but also a brilliant reinvention.
This is a sensational Broadway debut for an artist we'll hopefully be seeing more from in years to come.
Music supervisor Daniel Kluger, through new orchestrations and arrangements, has unearthed psychologically complex relationships among this band of settlers in turn-of-the-century “Indian Territory.”
And if you listen real hard, you’ll find that in this “Oklahoma!” like the rest of the modern world, no one really gets to ride off into the sunset.
And should you be an audience member who thinks he or she knows “Oklahoma!”, rest assured, your view of this classic musical will be just as transformed by this innovative production.

It took a member of ever more prominent and lauded school of auteur directing — immersive staging, contemporary settings, innovative casting, use of video — to give us a so drastically re-envisioned Oklahoma! that it almost feels more like a new show than a revival.

I’m grateful for having first seen Daniel Fish’s dark, hip and homey production of “Oklahoma!” at St. Ann’s Warehouse last year, because I can see how much improved it is now that it has transferred to Broadway.
Even the title song, usually imbued with the sunny, can-do optimism of the war era, becomes in this revelatory production less an anthem of pride than of stubborn defiance.
If this isn't the 'Oklahoma!' of one's dreams, it offers a strong vision that speaks to this moment.
Full of personality, comic ingenuity and powerhouse vocals, she gives a truly a showstopping performance.
I will put a handful of tracks from this onto my personal playlist, and they will sit nicely next to any Guaraldi in the mix.
Don’t expect sunny smiles or anything that resembles optimism in this depressing Oklahoma.
Instead, why don’t we all acknowledge that the 20th-century version is the one that will stand the test of time?

Fun is not joy, though, and too often in this Oklahoma! I found myself missing the sense of magic and transcendence that comes from seeing life, with all its pleasure and pain, elevated by this particular art form.
This is truly a bleak vision, one that may deserve its own musical.
But it is not a good enough reason for destroying such an historically and artistically magnificent work.
Sexually charged and presented with a striking naturalism, this bold new production is a revelation and a must-see.
Put plainly, this 'Oklahoma!' is a masterpiece in every element: direction, design, choreography, and acting; it has set the new gold standard on how to do a revival.
Oklahoma!'s eery timeliness is proof of the universality of the show.
It floats and sails with country jamboree-style through this inventive and daring revival

“Without considerable changes...Fish has totally reimagined the musical, infusing a whole new vision into the landmark show...For some, his pared-down version will be exhilarating; for those who love the original, the show will be disappointing and slow...Fish is baring the real emotions of his characters...
The first act is a joy from start to finish
Like the show as a whole, the dance demonstrates that there is much we can do to revivify these staid mid-century classics.
Violence and smoldering sexual desires are layered under the sunny lyrics of “Oh, What a Beautiful Mornin’,” unveiling a darkness this land has known since its earliest days.
For this viewer, though, Daniel Fish's Oklahoma! isn't doing fine at all, and it's certainly not OK.
This reimagining of “Oklahoma!” adds very little – if anything at all – to the original musical or any of its previous revivals.
Mr. Fish has stripped Oklahoma! of any breath, color, insight, delicacy, intimacy, choreography, costumes, subtle acting, and beautiful singing.

cn.t: Fish's stripped-down revival divides critics but mostly impresses with its dark, sexy reimagining that excavates violence beneath the classic's sunny surface. Bluegrass orchestrations and intimate staging earn praise, though some find it pretentious.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
